issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategies node mixes avoidance behaviours with what appears to be a trigger-like cue. 'Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' is phrased as a social reminder/trigger rather than a coping strategy, so within the specified node it is clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' and 'Avoid Intimacy' imply social withdrawal, which can fit PTSD, but the specific target 'seeing people that I socialised with before the event' suggests avoidance of trauma reminders tied to the past. This sits awkwardly with the selected Negative Appraisals, which focus on incapacity, moral injury, and not belonging, without any corresponding interpersonal mistrust, shame in relationships, or reminder-based social threat theme.

issues.item: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere
issues.explanation: 'Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere' is possible in PTSD, but here it leans toward a broad identity/interpersonal alienation theme that is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The Threat items are predominantly hypervigilant safety-checking and pursuit fears, while the other appraisal items emphasize incapacity and violated values; this makes the belonging item feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent appraisal cluster.

vignette:
Kenji, a twenty-six-year-old bank teller, described the past eight months as living in a different, more dangerous version of his own life. The world he knew had ended on a Tuesday afternoon during his lunch break. He was walking back to the bank when the first explosion tore through the plaza, shattering the glass-fronted lobby he was moments from entering. In the chaos that followed, amid the smoke and screaming, Kenji's only instinct was to run. He didn't stop to help, didn't look back; he just ran until his lungs burned, leaving behind the carnage and the face of a woman who had fallen near him. That image, and the shame of his flight, became the anchor for everything that followed.

In the weeks after the attack, a constant, humming sense of threat took root. He began waking up multiple times a night, his heart pounding, certain someone was in his apartment, forcing him to get up and check the locks on his doors and windows. His commute to work became an ordeal of vigilance; he found himself constantly looking over his shoulder, convinced he was being followed. This pervasive sense of danger was fueled by a deep and corrosive set of beliefs he had developed about himself. His conviction that he had acted cowardly, violating his own values by running, had metastasized into a certainty that he could no longer rely on himself in a crisis. This belief that he was fundamentally untrustworthy made him feel that danger was not just possible, but probable, and that he was uniquely unequipped to face it. This appraisal of his own inadequacy fed his hypervigilance, creating a world where every sudden noise was a threat and every stranger a potential assailant.

The constant state of alert, in turn, served as damning evidence for his negative self-appraisals. Every time he flinched at a car backfiring or snapped at his then-wife for startling him, it felt like a fresh confirmation of his own failure. He saw the fear in her eyes not as a product of his trauma, but as a judgment on his character, solidifying his belief that he was no longer the capable man she had married. His irritability grew into unpredictable bursts of anger, and the man who once prided himself on his calm demeanor became volatile and harsh. This transformation was the most painful proof that he was broken, cementing the appraisal that he couldn't rely on himself to be a good husband, or even a predictable person. Their marriage crumbled under the weight of it, and she left six months after the attack.

Alone in their old apartment, Kenji developed strategies to manage the overwhelming thoughts and feelings. He began taking every extra shift he could at the bank, working until he was too exhausted to think. The long hours spent counting cash and processing transactions provided a temporary reprieve from the memory of the woman's face and the sound of the explosion. In the evenings, he would actively try to suppress any thoughts of the trauma, turning the TV volume up to drown out the silence. He stopped returning calls from friends and deflected any attempts by his family to talk about how he was doing, avoiding any kind of emotional intimacy. These strategies, however, came at a cost. Each time he dodged a conversation or buried himself in work to avoid being alone, it felt like another admission of weakness. This pattern of avoidance reinforced his belief that he was no longer capable of connecting with people or managing his own mind, deepening the very shame he was trying to escape.

Kenji finally sought therapy after an incident at work. A heavy cash box was dropped behind him, and the loud bang sent him diving to the floor behind his counter, shouting in panic. The embarrassment was acute, but it was the look of pity from his manager that broke through his avoidance. He realized he couldn't keep living this way, a prisoner to a single moment. He is terrified that he is permanently damaged, but holds a fragile hope that he might one day walk down the street without looking back, and feel like himself again.
